items.followUp: Define a bonding pair of electrons and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of a lone pair.
rubric.description: Defines a lone pair as a pair of valence electrons not involved in bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Gives a valid example and identifies its lone pair(s).
rubric.description: Gives an example, such as oxygen in water having two lone pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A lone pair is a pair of valence electrons on an atom that is not shared with another atom in a chemical bond.
For example, the oxygen atom in a water molecule has two lone pairs.

items.followUp: Explain what happens to the rate of evaporation when temperature rises.

rubric.why: States the direction of the temperature effect.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Explains the effect in terms of particles escaping into the vapour.
rubric.description: Explains that higher kinetic energy allows more liquid molecules to escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure increases when the temperature of a liquid increases.
At a higher temperature, more molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape from the liquid into the vapour.

rubric.why: Shows that 24 carat represents pure gold.
rubric.description: States that 24-carat gold is pure gold.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as pure gold.

rubric.why: States the gold content of 24-carat gold.
rubric.description: States that all 24 parts out of 24 are gold (100% gold).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct composition.

modelAnswer: 24-carat gold is pure gold.
It contains 24 parts of gold out of 24 parts, so it is 100% gold.

items.followUp: How would you prepare 500 mL of a 1 M sodium chloride solution?

rubric.why: Gives the defining amount of solute and final solution volume for a 1 M solution.
rubric.description: States that a 1 M solution contains one mole of solute in one litre of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition or preparation quantity.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example using the molar mass of sodium chloride.
rubric.description: Gives the example of dissolving 58.5 g of NaCl and making the solution up to 1 L.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example and final volume.

modelAnswer: A one-molar (1 M) solution contains one mole of solute in one litre of solution.
Weigh 58.5 g of sodium chloride (NaCl), its molar mass, and dissolve it in a small amount of distilled water.
Transfer the solution to a 1 L volumetric flask and add distilled water up to the 1 L mark; mix well.

items.followUp: Define a homogeneous mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: Includes the essential description of a solution.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: Gives a valid example of a solution.
rubric.description: Gives an example, such as salt dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute and a solvent.
For example, salt dissolved in water is a solution.

items.followUp: A solution contains 12 g of solute in 80 g of solution. Calculate its mass/mass percentage.

rubric.why: Recognizes the correct quantities used in the definition.
rubric.description: States that mass/mass percentage is based on the mass of solute divided by the mass of solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct ratio.

rubric.why: Includes the multiplication by 100 required to express the ratio as a percentage.
rubric.description: States the formula: (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including the percentage factor.

modelAnswer: Mass/mass percentage is the mass of solute present in 100 parts by mass of the solution.
Mass/mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.

items.followUp: Name and give an example of each type of molecule classified by the number of atoms.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies a molecule consisting of one atom and gives an example.
rubric.description: Monoatomic molecule: one atom, e.g. helium (He).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and a suitable example.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies a molecule consisting of two atoms and gives an example.
rubric.description: Diatomic molecule: two atoms, e.g. hydrogen (H₂).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and a suitable example.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies a molecule consisting of three atoms and gives an example.
rubric.description: Triatomic molecule: three atoms, e.g. water (H₂O).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and a suitable example.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies a molecule consisting of more than three atoms and gives an example.
rubric.description: Polyatomic molecule: more than three atoms, e.g. ammonia (NH₃).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the type and a suitable example.

modelAnswer: Molecules may be classified by the number of atoms they contain:
1. Monoatomic: contains one atom; example: helium (He).
2. Diatomic: contains two atoms; example: hydrogen (H₂).
3. Triatomic: contains three atoms; example: water (H₂O).
4. Polyatomic: contains more than three atoms; example: ammonia (NH₃).

items.followUp: Use an electron dot-and-cross model to show the formation of magnesium oxide.

rubric.why: Defines the ionic bond as the attraction between the ions formed.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond as the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Identifies the electron transfer involved in the example.
rubric.description: Shows that a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct transfer.

rubric.why: Identifies the ions produced by electron transfer.
rubric.description: Shows formation of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both ions with the correct charges.

rubric.why: Shows that chlorine gains a stable outer electron shell.
rubric.description: Shows that the transferred electron completes chlorine's outer shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the completed outer shell in the dot-and-cross model.

rubric.why: Gives the resulting ionic compound and a suitable formation equation.
rubric.description: Writes the formation equation and identifies sodium chloride as the ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct equation and product.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
A sodium atom transfers its one outer electron to a chlorine atom.
Dot-and-cross model (× is sodium's electron; • are chlorine's electrons):
The transferred electron completes chlorine's outer shell; the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms the ionic bond in sodium chloride.
Overall equation: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
